events.title: Ruby 3.0 released
events.summary: Matz released Ruby 3.0 on December 25, 2020 — promising 3× faster performance versus Ruby 2.0 and introducing RBS static typing and fiber schedulers.
events.about: Ruby 3 aimed to keep Rails developers happy while answering speed criticism: YJIT (later), improved GC, and concurrent fibers for async I/O. RBS files let teams document types without changing Ruby's dynamic feel — a compromise before gradual typing in 3.x.

narrative.whyChosen: Ruby 3 was the language's answer to 'Ruby is too slow' after years of 2.x maintenance.
narrative.whyImportant: Performance work and RBS kept Ruby viable for Shopify-scale Rails deployments.
narrative.problemSolved: Ruby 2.7 warned the community that 3.0 would break compatibility unless they modernized gems and patterns.

events.title: C++20 standardized
events.summary: ISO published C++20 in December 2020 — adding concepts, coroutines, ranges, and the spaceship operator (`<=>`).
events.about: C++20 let compilers reject bad templates at the constraint level (concepts), write async code with coroutines, and chain range transformations fluently. It was the biggest standard since C++11 and influenced how modern C++ tutorials and codebases are written.

narrative.whyChosen: C++20 brought concepts and coroutines — features the standards committee had pursued for years.
narrative.whyImportant: Concepts improved template error messages and API design across the STL.
narrative.problemSolved: Template metaprogramming was powerful but unreadable; C++ needed safer, clearer abstractions.

events.title: Adobe Flash Player discontinued
events.summary: Adobe ended Flash Player distribution and updates on December 31, 2020 — ending ActionScript's run as a browser programming platform.
events.about: Flash Player had powered browser games, video players, and interactive ads for two decades. After this date Adobe stopped security patches and blocked Flash content from running in the plugin (January 12, 2021). Developers who had built on ActionScript migrated to HTML5 canvas, WebGL, and JavaScript — or lost access to legacy `.swf` content entirely.

narrative.whyChosen: Flash Player's shutdown closed the ActionScript era and marked HTML5's victory for in-browser media.
narrative.whyImportant: It broke millions of legacy games, training modules, and corporate sites that still depended on the plugin.
narrative.problemSolved: Flash's security record and plugin model no longer fit a web platform moving to open standards.

events.title: FTC sues Facebook for anticompetitive conduct
events.summary: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission filed an antitrust lawsuit against Facebook on December 9, 2020 — alleging illegal monopolization through acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp and anticompetitive platform policies.
events.about: The suit sought divestitures of Instagram and WhatsApp — unprecedented for a social platform. It ran parallel to state AG cases and EU DMA designations, signaling a new era of antitrust aimed at network-effect moats rather than just price fixing. Developers watched for mandates to open social graphs, interoperability APIs, and reduced platform self-preferencing.

narrative.whyChosen: The FTC suit was the boldest U.S. antitrust challenge to a social platform since Microsoft.
narrative.whyImportant: It threatened breakups of Instagram and WhatsApp and reshaped M&A calculus for big tech.
narrative.problemSolved: Regulators argued Facebook bought rivals to maintain monopoly power in social networking.

events.title: SolarWinds supply-chain hack disclosed
events.summary: FireEye disclosed on December 13, 2020 that nation-state actors had compromised SolarWinds Orion software — inserting backdoor code into updates trusted by thousands of organizations.
events.about: The SUNBURST trojan rode signed Orion builds into U.S. government agencies, Microsoft, and Fortune 500 networks — the definitive supply-chain breach. DevOps teams accelerated SBOM adoption, build-pipeline signing, and least-privilege for CI/CD — treating dependency and vendor updates as attack surfaces, not chores.

narrative.whyChosen: SolarWinds was the supply-chain compromise that made every vendor update suspect.
narrative.whyImportant: It forced SBOMs, signed builds, and zero-trust into mainstream DevSecOps.
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing initially — attackers piggybacked on trusted auto-update channels.
